name: Proanthocyanidins (PAC) supplements
short: Cranberry juice (not PAC itself): major bleeding on warfarin in a case report; a trial found no important effect. Mice: polymeric PAC caused liver inflammation. Women with UTI: PAC side effects low.
text: Proanthocyanidin supplements by mouth, source not stated: in a multicentre double-blind trial in women with recurrent urinary tract infections that compared a prolonged-release D-mannose product that also contained proanthocyanidins, ursolic acid, vitamins A, C and D and zinc against proanthocyanidins alone (valid data from 93 women; the 2020 report describes both as daily oral sachets), the incidence of side effects was low and diarrhoea was the most frequent side effect in both groups; the later report of the same comparison (283 women included, valid data from 184) gives no adverse-event figures. Cranberry proanthocyanidin extracts: in a 12-month placebo-controlled trial in women with recurrent cystitis (172 enrolled, 160 analysed), no adverse events were reported, and in a 24-week trial in 145 women comparing a high with a low dose, no major side effects were reported. A 2023 Cochrane review of cranberry products, which contain proanthocyanidins (50 studies, 8,857 participants), found that the number of people with gastrointestinal side effects probably does not differ from placebo or no treatment (10 studies, 2,166 participants; risk ratio 1.33, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.77). These cranberry data apply to cranberry-derived products; the abstracts of the page's trials do not say where their proanthocyanidins came from. Liver (animal data only): polymeric proanthocyanidins caused liver injury, described as nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, in mice, by increasing the liver's exposure to gut bacterial toxins; the authors say their toxicity needs critical evaluation for human consumption. Warfarin (cranberry products; none of these sources tested proanthocyanidin supplements as such): a case report describes major bleeding and a high INR in a patient on stable warfarin soon after he started daily cranberry juice, with no other identifiable reason for the high INR. In a randomised double-blind trial in 30 patients on stable warfarin, 240 mL of cranberry juice a day for 2 weeks did not change warfarin blood levels, and a small INR difference at a single time point was judged unlikely to be clinically important. A 2021 safety review identified warfarin interactions as a potential risk of cranberry; it reports that moderate juice intakes (240 to 480 mL) were not associated with interactions, that some reports suggested an interaction requires excessive intakes (1 to 2 L of juice or 3,000 mg of cranberry extract a day), and that cases mostly involved patients with serious illnesses or taking other medicines.
